title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection

paper.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
paper.abstract:
Abstract Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy’s competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention.
Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables language-model agents to improve through multi-turn interaction with verifiable environments, but long horizons and sparse outcome rewards make successful behavior difficult to discover and reinforce ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . Textual skills can ease this challenge by compressing trajectories or feedback into reusable procedural guidance for subsequent decisions ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Existing approaches extract, refine, and retrieve such guidance using external memory or teacher models ( Nottingham et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . SkillRL, for example, uses a stronger teacher to build an evolving SkillBank, turning sparse trajectory-level feedback into guidance for subsequent exploration ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: Overview and empirical summary of SkillScaffold . Low-cost, policy-relative skill-utility estimates guide selective skill injection during training, while inference remains skill-free. Across four agentic benchmarks, SkillScaffold consistently outperforms GRPO and SkillRL while injecting skills for only a small fraction of training queries. Recent work shows that a shared policy can generate skills from experience and use them for subsequent problem solving, allowing generation and execution capabilities to co-evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work internalizes skill-conditioned behavior via curriculum learning or self-distillation, enabling skill-free inference ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Building on these directions, we study skills as policy-adaptive training scaffolds , focusing on evaluating and selectively using guidance for the current policy and query. Under this training-time scaffold view, skill credit assignment uses a scalar skill utility for each candidate to determine whether any skill should be used and which one to select. Existing approaches either use generated skills without testing their benefit ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , rely on indirect and delayed feedback ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or estimate utility through additional skill-conditioned environment rollouts ( Fan et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . Our pilot studies show that rollout-based estimates are costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and with how reliably the current policy solves each query without skills ( Dong et al., 2026a ) . These findings motivate a low-cost, policy-relative utility signal for candidate ranking and abstention. To address these challenges, we propose SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold for agentic RL, summarized in Figure 1 . Its core idea is to replace candidate-specific environment evaluation with outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing training trajectories. A shared policy serves as both an Executor , which collects skill-free Scout trajectories, and a Generator , which produces candidate skills from outcome-labeled Scout evidence. For each candidate, SkillScaffold rescores fixed Scout evidence under candidate-skill and no-skill contexts to obtain a policy-relative utility estimate. This proxy favors increased likelihood of successful behavior and reduced likelihood of observed failures, according to the available outcome evidence. The highest-utility candidate guides fresh Executor rollouts only when its estimated utility is positive; otherwise, execution remains skill-free. Environment rewards supervise the Executor, while skill utility supervises the Generator through role-specific GRPO objectives, enabling the Generator to adapt its guidance to the evolving Executor. Skill-free Scouts and selectively scaffolded Executor trajectories jointly update the shared policy, encouraging skill internalization. At deployment, the Generator and the entire skill pathway are removed. We evaluate SkillScaffold on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench, covering diverse multi-turn environments. Across these settings, SkillScaffold improves over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under fully skill-free inference. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. In summary, the key contributions of this work are as follows: • We identify two key challenges in skill credit assignment: rollout-based evaluation is costly and unstable, while skill benefits depend on both the candidate and how reliably the current policy can solve the query without skills, motivating candidate ranking and abstention. • We propose SkillScaffold , a shared-policy training scaffold that estimates candidate utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing trajectories. The resulting signal guides skill selection, abstention, and Generator learning without candidate-specific environment rollouts. • Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench demonstrate improvements over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under skill-free inference. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention.

sections.heading: 3 Motivating Observations
sections.text: Skill-based agentic RL must decide whether and which generated skill should guide subsequent exploration. Rollout-based utility estimation is costly and unstable under practical sampling budgets, while skill utility varies across candidates and with the current policy. We first characterize these two challenges before introducing SkillScaffold .

sections.heading: 3.1 Rollout-Based Skill-Utility Estimation Is Unstable and Costly
sections.text: For a task x x with M M candidate skills 𝒞 x = { s i } i = 1 M \mathcal{C}_{x}=\{s_{i}\}_{i=1}^{M} , direct skill utility is the downstream improvement over skill-free execution: U DR ( s ; x ) = 𝔼 τ ∼ π θ exec ( ⋅ ∣ x , s ; 𝒯 ) [ R ( τ ; x ) ] − 𝔼 τ ∼ π θ exec ( ⋅ ∣ x , ∅ ; 𝒯 ) [ R ( τ ; x ) ] . U_{\mathrm{DR}}(s;x)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{exec}}(\cdot\mid x,s;\mathcal{T})}[R(\tau;x)]-\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\mathrm{exec}}(\cdot\mid x,\varnothing;\mathcal{T})}[R(\tau;x)]. (4) Estimating each condition with K K episodes and sharing the skill-free baseline requires ( M + 1 ) ​ K (M+1)K additional environment rollouts per query.

sections.heading: Pilot observation.
sections.text: For each candidate–query pair and budget K K , we form two independent estimates of U DR U_{\mathrm{DR}} and record a sign disagreement when both are non-zero but have opposite signs. Figure 2 (a) shows that disagreement decreases only from 23 % 23\% at K = 1 K=1 to 16 % 16\% at K = 8 K=8 under sparse outcome rewards. Figure 2: Rollout-based utility estimation is costly and unstable. (a) Sign disagreement between independent estimates. (b) More rollout samples distinguish more candidate groups. A query-level candidate group is non-tied when its M M candidates do not all receive the same empirical utility. Figure 2 (b) shows that increasing the additional rollout budget eight-fold, from 5 5 to 40 40 per query, raises the fraction of non-tied groups only from 32 % 32\% to 55 % 55\% , leaving nearly half unresolved. Online RL must immediately decide whether and which skill to inject, whereas reliable candidate-specific estimates require additional interaction. We therefore seek a low-cost utility estimate that avoids candidate-specific downstream rollouts.

sections.heading: 3.2 Skill Utility Is Query- and Policy-Dependent
sections.text: Low interaction cost alone is insufficient: skill utility varies across queries, candidates, and policy competence, so credit assignment must both rank candidates and abstain when none is helpful. Figure 3: Skill utility is query- and policy-dependent. (a) Candidate effects vary within a query. (b) Skill benefit decreases as skill-free policy competence improves.

sections.heading: Within-query variation.
sections.text: On a non-saturated pilot subset where candidate differences remain measurable, Figure 3 (a) compares the best and worst observed candidates for each query, as measured by downstream rollouts relative to skill-free execution. Among 100 100 queries, 28 28 contain both positive- and negative-effect candidates, showing that generating plausible skills is insufficient; candidates must be distinguished at the query level.

sections.heading: Dependence on policy competence.
sections.text: We measure current competence using four independent skill-free probe rollouts from the same frozen policy. Here, a probe is an evaluation-only rollout used to assess the policy’s current skill-free competence. This avoids conflation with historical training-time Scout outcomes. We group queries by their number of successful probes ( 0 0 – 4 4 ). Figure 3 (b) reports both the mean candidate effect and the best observed candidate. Average skill gains are positive when only a minority of probes succeed; when most or all succeed, the mean effect becomes negative and even the best observed candidate provides little or no additional benefit. Thus, skill credit assignment requires a query- and policy-relative utility to identify the most helpful candidate and abstain when none provides positive additional value. These downstream measurements are used only for diagnosis, not as training signals for SkillScaffold .

sections.heading: 4 SkillScaffold
sections.text: SkillScaffold uses one shared policy π θ \pi_{\theta} in two roles: the Executor interacts with the environment, while the Generator produces candidate skills from outcome-labeled trajectories. As shown in Figure 4 , each update collects skill-free Scouts, generates and scores candidate skills, and injects only the highest-utility positive candidate into fresh Executor rollouts. Environment rewards train the Executor, skill utility trains the Generator, and their shared parameters enable fully skill-free deployment.

sections.heading: Group-based evidence.
sections.text: The Generator receives the task and all outcome-labeled Scouts. It extracts reusable decisions from all-success groups, diagnoses recurring errors from all-failure groups, and contrasts successful and failed behavior in mixed groups. Thus, both successes and failures provide query-specific evidence for skill generation.

A useful skill should be compatible with verified successful behavior and incompatible with observed failed behavior. Directly testing this criterion with fresh environment rollouts would reproduce the cost and variance identified in Section 3.1 . Instead, we keep the Scouts fixed and compare how the current policy scores the same behavior with and without each candidate skill.

sections.heading: Skill-free deployment.
sections.text: At deployment, we disable the skill pathway and use π θ ∗ exec ( ⋅ ∣ x , ∅ , h t ; 𝒯 ) \pi_{\theta^{*}}^{\mathrm{exec}}(\cdot\mid x,\varnothing,h_{t};\mathcal{T}) , eliminating Scout collection and all skill-related inference overhead.

sections.heading: Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate SkillScaffold on four interactive benchmarks. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) is a text-based household environment requiring multi-step planning and object interaction. WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022a ) is an online-shopping simulator in which agents search for products matching user specifications. ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) evaluates interactive scientific reasoning and experimentation. These three are short-horizon settings. In contrast, τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench ( Yao et al., 2024 ) evaluates long-horizon tool-agent-user interaction across Airline, Retail, and Telecom. We report success rate for the first three benchmarks and Pass@1 for τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench. Dataset and evaluation details are provided in Appendix A.1 .

sections.heading: Baselines and Implementation Details.
sections.text: All main runs use Qwen3-8B. Baselines include (1) Prompt- and memory-based methods: ReAct ( Yao et al., 2022b ) , Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , Mem0 ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , ExpeL ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , MemP ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , and direct skill prompting. (2) RL methods: GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2026 ) optimize the policy without skill augmentation. (3) Skill-based RL methods: INSPO ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) and SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026 ) use teacher-generated guidance, whereas Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , Evolving-RL ( Fan et al., 2026 ) , and SEED ( Wu et al., 2026 ) generate or distill guidance from the policy’s own experience. Full implementation details are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Overall performance.
sections.text: Tables 1 and 2 show a clear progression over increasingly competitive baselines. First, SkillScaffold substantially outperforms prompt- and memory-based methods, with gains of 23.5 points on WebShop and 49.6 on ALFWorld over their strongest results. It then surpasses standard RL methods across all four benchmarks, including gains of 9.2 points on ALFWorld and 4.2 on ScienceWorld. Finally, SkillScaffold remains best against skill-based RL methods on every benchmark, improving the strongest such results by 3.3 points on WebShop and 3.0 on ALFWorld. Its 6.3-point gain on Telecom further extends this advantage to long-horizon tool use. Full training dynamics are provided in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Skill-free deployment and generalization.
sections.text: SkillScaffold removes the Generator and all textual skills at inference, yet outperforms skill-conditioned baselines on both WebShop and ALFWorld. On WebShop, it reaches 45.1 without skills, compared with 41.8 for Evolving-RL with skills and 27.7 after its skills are removed. The gains also hold across ID and OOD splits: SkillScaffold reaches 46.6/42.0 on WebShop and 96.2/48.8 on ScienceWorld, exceeding the strongest competing results on both splits. Thus, the improvements do not rely on retaining an external skill pathway and generalize beyond the training categories. Full Pass@ k k results are provided in Appendix Table 6 . sections.text: Table 3: Ablation results on ALFWorld and WebShop. Variant ALF. Web. SkillScaffold (Full) 94.8 45.1 Generator Learning w/o Generator learning 89.6 39.5 No Gen. loss + random selection 81.3 40.3 Utility Selection Random selection 79.9 39.2 Shuffled utility 82.8 37.1 Selective Scaffolding w/o abstention 85.8 39.6 No Executor injection 90.3 41.5 Table 3 isolates utility-supervised Generator learning, utility-based candidate selection, and positive-gated skill injection. Removing Generator learning reduces ALFWorld/WebShop performance to 89.6/39.5, showing that skill generation must adapt to the evolving policy. Random selection and shuffled candidate–utility assignments yield 79.9/39.2 and 82.8/37.1, showing that utility must both guide selection and remain paired with the candidate it evaluates. sections.heading: 5.4 Validating Skill Utility for Credit Assignment
sections.text: Figure 5: Skill-utility validation. We reuse the independently evaluated query–candidate sets from the pilot study. For each candidate, the likelihood-based utility is computed only from the fixed Scout trajectories, without using its downstream evaluation rollouts. Figure 5 (a) applies four decision rules to the same candidate sets: skill-free execution, random injection, forced injection of the utility-ranked top-1 candidate, and top-1 injection only when its utility is positive. Their success rates are 61.8%, 60.1%, 63.0%, and 67.6%, respectively. This shows that ranking alone provides only a modest gain, whereas positive gating is critical for avoiding unhelpful or harmful injections. Panel (b) partitions candidate–query pairs into five utility quintiles and uses independent downstream rollouts only for evaluation, reporting gain over skill-free execution. The measured gain rises with utility, supporting its use for both ranking and abstention.

sections.heading: 5.5 SkillScaffold Improves Training-Time Exploration

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold for skill credit assignment in agentic RL. Rather than assuming generated skills are helpful or evaluating every candidate through additional environment interaction, SkillScaffold reuses outcome-verified trajectories to estimate policy-relative utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons. This signal supports candidate ranking, abstention, and Generator learning, while environment outcomes continue to supervise the Executor. Across diverse short- and long-horizon benchmarks, SkillScaffold improves over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under fully skill-free inference. Overall, SkillScaffold selectively uses skills to improve training-time exploration, absorbs their guidance into the policy, and removes the skill pathway at deployment.

sections.heading: ALFWorld.
sections.text: ALFWorld contains six household task categories: Pick, Heat, Cool, Clean, Look, and Pick2. We train on the full 3,553-task split, comprising 790 Pick, 459 Heat, 533 Cool, 650 Clean, 308 Look, and 813 Pick2 tasks, and evaluate success rate on the 134-task valid-unseen split.

sections.heading: WebShop.
sections.text: Following the category-generalization protocol of Skill0.5 ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , we partition the 12,087 human-annotated WebShop goals into seven domains using keyword-based classification of goal instructions. Apparel, Electronics, Footwear, and Other are used for training and ID evaluation; Accessories, Beauty & Health, and Home Decor are held out for OOD evaluation. Because Other initially accounts for over 60% of the goals, we apply farthest-point sampling over sentence embeddings to balance its size. The resulting training split contains 3,320 ID goals: 776 Apparel, 938 Electronics, 606 Footwear, and 1,000 Other goals, with Other downsampled from approximately 6,600. The ID validation split contains 454 goals: 113 Apparel, 152 Electronics, 89 Footwear, and 100 Other, with Other downsampled from approximately 940. The OOD validation split contains 207 goals: 80 Accessories, 54 Beauty & Health, and 73 Home Decor. Training uses original goal indices 1,500 onward, while the validation pool combines the original test indices 0–499 and development indices 500–1,499.

sections.heading: ScienceWorld.
sections.text: Following ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) , we use the electricity split, which contains two task types: identifying power components and testing conductivity. The action space contains approximately 26 verb templates, and the interaction horizon is at most 50 steps. Training uses 460 variations: 10 power-component and 450 test-conductivity variations under the easy simplification. Test-ID uses 230 development episodes with held-out variations of the same task types; Test-OOD uses 155 episodes from related variants involving unknown-material conductivity and renewable energy. We report ID and OOD success rates.

sections.heading: τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench.
sections.text: τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench evaluates long-horizon dialogue, tool execution, and policy compliance in Airline, Retail, and Telecom. Unlike the other three benchmarks, all RL-based baselines and SkillScaffold are trained from the same SFT checkpoint. The user role is simulated by DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Both the SFT and RL data are derived from the synthetic data released by AReaL-SEA ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . We estimate task pass rates with the SFT model and remove all-success and all-failure groups, which provide no group-relative learning signal. The resulting RL pool contains 300 entries per domain, or 900 in total.

sections.heading: A.4 Evidence Construction and Candidate Generation
sections.text: For group-based training, the evidence record contains the task, all N N Scout trajectories, and their verifier outcomes. All-success groups emphasize reusable successful decisions, all-failure groups request conditional corrections without inventing an unobserved solution, and mixed groups contrast successful and failed decisions. For anchor-based training, the first verified successful Scout in sampling order is used as the evidence anchor. If no Scout succeeds, candidate generation and Generator optimization are skipped for that query, and Executor execution remains skill-free. Each evidence record produces M M independently sampled candidate skills. Candidates must satisfy the prescribed card format and express reusable decision guidance rather than copy task-specific answers. Formatting validity is checked separately from utility availability: an invalid candidate is never selected, while an incomplete Generator group is omitted according to the rules in Section 4.5 .

sections.heading: Skill-utility validation.
sections.text: The comparison in Section 5.4 applies every injection rule to the same fixed query–candidate sets. Candidate utilities are computed from the fixed Scout trajectories, while separate downstream rollouts are reserved for evaluation. The utility-quintile analysis groups candidate–query pairs by the estimated utility and reports their independently measured gain over skill-free execution.

sections.heading: Skill-free strategy acquisition.
sections.text: For each benchmark, we form a fixed cohort at an early checkpoint from training queries that benefit from skill-assisted exploration. Cohort membership is frozen before later evaluation. The same queries are then reevaluated at a later checkpoint with the skill pathway disabled, and recovery is computed as the later-minus-early skill-free success rate. Confidence intervals use a query-level bootstrap.

(18) If U ^ j ^ > 0 \widehat{U}_{\widehat{j}}>0 , the error bound gives U j ^ > − ε U_{\widehat{j}}>-\varepsilon . If every estimated utility is nonpositive, then U j ≤ U ^ j + ε ≤ ε U_{j}\leq\widehat{U}_{j}+\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon for every candidate. □ \square The proposition formalizes two roles of utility in skill credit assignment. Ranking incurs at most 2 ​ ε 2\varepsilon proxy regret, while abstention avoids overlooking any candidate whose proxy advantage exceeds the estimation-error scale.

sections.heading: C.4 Interaction and Computation Complexity
sections.text: With M M candidates and K K evaluation episodes per condition, direct rollout utility estimation requires ( M + 1 ) ​ K (M+1)K additional environment trajectories per query when the skill-free condition is shared. SkillScaffold launches no candidate-specific environment trajectories. It reuses N N Scouts already collected for training and requires M ​ N MN candidate-conditioned trajectory scores plus N N cached skill-free scores, giving 𝒪 ⁡ ( M ​ N ) \mathcal{O}(MN) additional model scoring work. After selection, the L L post-selection trajectories are ordinary Executor training data rather than candidate-evaluation rollouts. With the default N = M = L = 4 N=M=L=4 , each update uses eight environment trajectories in the Executor group and twenty reusable trajectory-context scores for utility computation.

Affiliation: Zhejiang University Kun Kuang 2 2 footnotemark: 2 Affiliation: Zhejiang University Abstract Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy’s competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates candidate skills and estimates their utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons, without candidate-specific environment rollouts. The resulting utility guides whether and which skill to inject, retaining skill-free execution when no candidate is estimated to help. Joint training enables the Generator to produce skills tailored to the evolving Executor. Scaffolded RL encourages skill internalization for skill-free inference. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench demonstrate gains over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines across both short- and long-horizon tasks. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. Our code is available at https://github.com/Vaidurya00/SkillScaffold . 1 Introduction Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables language-model agents to improve through multi-turn interaction with verifiable environments, but long horizons and sparse outcome rewards make successful behavior difficult to discover and reinforce ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . Textual skills can ease this challenge by compressing trajectories or feedback into reusable procedural guidance for subsequent decisions ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Existing approaches extract, refine, and retrieve such guidance using external memory or teacher models ( Nottingham et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . SkillRL, for example, uses a stronger teacher to build an evolving SkillBank, turning sparse trajectory-level feedback into guidance for subsequent exploration ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . Figure 1: Overview and empirical summary of SkillScaffold . Low-cost, policy-relative skill-utility estimates guide selective skill injection during training, while inference remains skill-free. Across four agentic benchmarks, SkillScaffold consistently outperforms GRPO and SkillRL while injecting skills for only a small fraction of training queries. Recent work shows that a shared policy can generate skills from experience and use them for subsequent problem solving, allowing generation and execution capabilities to co-evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Xia et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work internalizes skill-conditioned behavior via curriculum learning or self-distillation, enabling skill-free inference ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . Building on these directions, we study skills as policy-adaptive training scaffolds , focusing on evaluating and selectively using guidance for the current policy and query. Under this training-time scaffold view, skill credit assignment uses a scalar skill utility for each candidate to determine whether any skill should be used and which one to select. Existing approaches either use generated skills without testing their benefit ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , rely on indirect and delayed feedback ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or estimate utility through additional skill-conditioned environment rollouts ( Fan et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . Our pilot studies show that rollout-based estimates are costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and with how reliably the current policy solves each query without skills ( Dong et al., 2026a ) . These findings motivate a low-cost, policy-relative utility signal for candidate ranking and abstention. To address these challenges, we propose SkillScaffold , a policy-adaptive training scaffold for agentic RL, summarized in Figure 1 . Its core idea is to replace candidate-specific environment evaluation with outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing training trajectories. A shared policy serves as both an Executor , which collects skill-free Scout trajectories, and a Generator , which produces candidate skills from outcome-labeled Scout evidence. For each candidate, SkillScaffold rescores fixed Scout evidence under candidate-skill and no-skill contexts to obtain a policy-relative utility estimate. This proxy favors increased likelihood of successful behavior and reduced likelihood of observed failures, according to the available outcome evidence. The highest-utility candidate guides fresh Executor rollouts only when its estimated utility is positive; otherwise, execution remains skill-free. Environment rewards supervise the Executor, while skill utility supervises the Generator through role-specific GRPO objectives, enabling the Generator to adapt its guidance to the evolving Executor. Skill-free Scouts and selectively scaffolded Executor trajectories jointly update the shared policy, encouraging skill internalization. At deployment, the Generator and the entire skill pathway are removed. We evaluate SkillScaffold on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench, covering diverse multi-turn environments. Across these settings, SkillScaffold improves over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under fully skill-free inference. Ablations and further analyses support the importance of utility-based selection and abstention. In summary, the key contributions of this work are as follows: • We identify two key challenges in skill credit assignment: rollout-based evaluation is costly and unstable, while skill benefits depend on both the candidate and how reliably the current policy can solve the query without skills, motivating candidate ranking and abstention. • We propose SkillScaffold , a shared-policy training scaffold that estimates candidate utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons on existing trajectories. The resulting signal guides skill selection, abstention, and Generator learning without candidate-specific environment rollouts. • Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, and τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench demonstrate improvements over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under skill-free inference. Rather than assuming generated skills are helpful or evaluating every candidate through additional environment interaction, SkillScaffold reuses outcome-verified trajectories to estimate policy-relative utility through outcome-aware likelihood comparisons. This signal supports candidate ranking, abstention, and Generator learning, while environment outcomes continue to supervise the Executor. Across diverse short- and long-horizon benchmarks, SkillScaffold improves over strong agentic-RL and skill-based RL baselines under fully skill-free inference. Overall, SkillScaffold selectively uses skills to improve training-time exploration, absorbs their guidance into the policy, and removes the skill pathway at deployment. Appendix A Implementation Details A.1 Benchmark and Data Details ALFWorld. ALFWorld contains six household task categories: Pick, Heat, Cool, Clean, Look, and Pick2. We train on the full 3,553-task split, comprising 790 Pick, 459 Heat, 533 Cool, 650 Clean, 308 Look, and 813 Pick2 tasks, and evaluate success rate on the 134-task valid-unseen split. WebShop. Following the category-generalization protocol of Skill0.5 ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , we partition the 12,087 human-annotated WebShop goals into seven domains using keyword-based classification of goal instructions. Apparel, Electronics, Footwear, and Other are used for training and ID evaluation; Accessories, Beauty & Health, and Home Decor are held out for OOD evaluation. Because Other initially accounts for over 60% of the goals, we apply farthest-point sampling over sentence embeddings to balance its size. The resulting training split contains 3,320 ID goals: 776 Apparel, 938 Electronics, 606 Footwear, and 1,000 Other goals, with Other downsampled from approximately 6,600. The ID validation split contains 454 goals: 113 Apparel, 152 Electronics, 89 Footwear, and 100 Other, with Other downsampled from approximately 940. The OOD validation split contains 207 goals: 80 Accessories, 54 Beauty & Health, and 73 Home Decor. Training uses original goal indices 1,500 onward, while the validation pool combines the original test indices 0–499 and development indices 500–1,499. ScienceWorld. Following ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) , we use the electricity split, which contains two task types: identifying power components and testing conductivity. The action space contains approximately 26 verb templates, and the interaction horizon is at most 50 steps. Training uses 460 variations: 10 power-component and 450 test-conductivity variations under the easy simplification. Test-ID uses 230 development episodes with held-out variations of the same task types; Test-OOD uses 155 episodes from related variants involving unknown-material conductivity and renewable energy. All-success groups emphasize reusable successful decisions, all-failure groups request conditional corrections without inventing an unobserved solution, and mixed groups contrast successful and failed decisions. For anchor-based training, the first verified successful Scout in sampling order is used as the evidence anchor. If no Scout succeeds, candidate generation and Generator optimization are skipped for that query, and Executor execution remains skill-free. Each evidence record produces M M independently sampled candidate skills. Candidates must satisfy the prescribed card format and express reusable decision guidance rather than copy task-specific answers. Formatting validity is checked separately from utility availability: an invalid candidate is never selected, while an incomplete Generator group is omitted according to the rules in Section 4.5 . A.5 Diagnostic Evaluation Protocols Skill-utility validation. The comparison in Section 5.4 applies every injection rule to the same fixed query–candidate sets. Candidate utilities are computed from the fixed Scout trajectories, while separate downstream rollouts are reserved for evaluation. The utility-quintile analysis groups candidate–query pairs by the estimated utility and reports their independently measured gain over skill-free execution. Skill-free strategy acquisition. For each benchmark, we form a fixed cohort at an early checkpoint from training queries that benefit from skill-assisted exploration. Cohort membership is frozen before later evaluation. The same queries are then reevaluated at a later checkpoint with the skill pathway disabled, and recovery is computed as the later-minus-early skill-free success rate. Confidence intervals use a query-level bootstrap.
